# Lab overview

**Date:** Fri 20 Nov 2026, on-site (MAD 024, 11:15–12:45)
**Deck:** `content/material/slides/E9-AICoding.qmd` (figures:
`slides/figures/E9/make-figures.R`)
**What students download:** `lab09.zip` — an R project with the worksheet
`lab09_worksheet.qmd`, the chart template `chart_template.R` and the data in
`data/gdplifexp2007.csv` (`DataScienceExercises::gdplifexp2007` from session 8,
exported as CSV). Rebuild the zip with `make-lab09-zip.sh` after any change to
`_student_template.qmd`, `chart_template.R` or `data/`.
**Students need:** laptop, R with `ggplot2` and `dplyr`, and any free AI chat
assistant in the browser.

## Timing

| Time | Block | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 0–5 | Goals · the rule from lecture 2 · four Ds | |
| 5–12 | Delegation | the trade-off slide is the core message |
| 12–20 | Description | vague prompt → good prompt → template |
| 20–28 | Discernment | weighted mean; the "25 years" number; four steps |
| 28–30 | Diligence · exercise instructions | assign routes P and T |
| 30–40 | Round 1 · just ask | |
| 40–55 | Round 2 · two routes | walk round; route T may ask small questions only |
| 55–65 | Round 3 · check and own | push for `count()` before the title |
| 65–80 | Sharing | minutes per route on the board; four questions on the slide |
| 80–85 | Summary | |

The exercise blocks (rounds 1–3 plus sharing) add up to about 50 minutes. If
the input runs long, shorten round 3 to `n` + title and skip the declaration.

## Assigning the routes

Split the room into halves: one half takes **route P** (good prompt), the
other **route T** (the chart template; session 8 showed similar code but students did not save a template of their own). The comparison in the sharing round
only works if both routes are represented. Fast pairs do the other route
(⭐ b).

# What to expect in each round

## Round 1 · just ask

Typical outcomes from a one-sentence prompt:

- `library(gapminder)` and `gapminder` instead of `gdp_data` — all twelve
  years, 1,704 rows, or an error if the package is not installed
- a `read.csv("gapminder.csv")` of a file that does not exist
- a bar chart of the **mean** life expectancy per continent — answers a
  different question (no variation, no countries)
- a sentence such as *"Africa has the lowest and most unequal life
  expectancy"* — half wrong, see below

## Round 2 · what a good answer looks like

Route T, finished: the chart template with the `# <- CHANGE` lines adapted.

```{r}
#| label: solution
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

gdp_data <- read.csv("data/gdplifexp2007.csv")

base_size <- 14   # font size of the whole chart: larger for slides
edge_space <- expansion(mult = 0.1)  # 10% extra room at both ends of the
                                     # x-axis, so that no label is cut off


# 1. The number for the title -- computed, never typed ----------------------

spread <- gdp_data |>
  group_by(continent) |>
  summarise(range = max(lifeExp) - min(lifeExp))      # <- CHANGE

asia_range <- spread$range[spread$continent == "Asia"]    # <- CHANGE


# 2. The countries that get a label: one per continent ----------------------

label_data <- gdp_data |>
  group_by(continent) |>
  slice_min(lifeExp, n = 1)    # <- CHANGE: slice_max() = highest,
                                 #    slice_min() = lowest


# 3. The chart ---------------------------------------------------------------

my_chart <- ggplot(
  data = gdp_data,
  # the variable on x, the groups on y: long group names stay readable
  mapping = aes(x = lifeExp, y = continent)              # <- CHANGE
) +
  # the box: median, middle half of the countries, and the range.
  # outlier.shape = NA hides the box's own outlier dots, because the
  # points below show every country anyway
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.6, colour = "grey50") +
  # every country as one point; alpha = 0.4 makes them see-through, so
  # where many countries overlap, the colour gets darker
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 2.5, colour = "#00395B") +
  # the labelled countries again, on top and in red ...
  geom_point(data = label_data, size = 3, colour = "#E65032") +
  # ... and their names, placed just above each box
  geom_text(
    data = label_data, mapping = aes(label = country),
    nudge_y = 0.4, size = base_size / 3.5, colour = "#E65032") +

  # x-axis: keep ONE of the two lines, put a # in front of the other.
  # log axis: for skewed variables such as income or population
  # scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1), expand = edge_space) +
  # linear axis: for most other variables, e.g. life expectancy
  scale_x_continuous(expand = edge_space) +

  labs(
    # the title states the finding, with the number computed above
    title = paste0("Life expectancy varies by ", round(asia_range),
                   " years within Asia"),      # <- CHANGE
    subtitle = "Life expectancy, 142 countries, 2007; red: lowest per continent",     # <- CHANGE
    x = "Life expectancy in years",                     # <- CHANGE: with unit
    y = NULL,                       # the continent names speak for themselves
    caption = "Data: Gapminder."    # always name the source
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
  theme(
    plot.title            = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.title.position   = "plot",     # title flush with the left edge
    plot.caption          = element_text(colour = "grey45", hjust = 1),
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    panel.grid.minor      = element_blank(),  # fewer lines, less clutter
    legend.position       = "top",      # if you add a legend: on top, left
    legend.justification  = "left"
  )

my_chart
```

Route T changes from the template: `lifeExp` instead of `gdpPercap` (mapping,
`summarise()`, labels); `slice_min()` instead of `slice_max()`; the
`scale_x_continuous()` line instead of `scale_x_log10()`; a difference instead
of a ratio in the title; new subtitle and axis label. The template already
has the right chart type, so a pair that reads the comments should get a
chart it can hand in within 15 minutes — that is deliberate: route T should
show that a good template gets you there without frustration.

Route P usually produces a vertical box plot (continents on x) with
`geom_jitter()`, which is fine; check whether the labels sit on the right
points and whether Oceania (n = 2) gets a box.

## Round 3 · the numbers to check against

```{r}
#| label: numbers
gdp_data |>
  group_by(continent) |>
  summarise(n = n(), lowest = min(lifeExp), median = median(lifeExp),
            highest = max(lifeExp), range = highest - lowest)
label_data |> select(continent, country, lifeExp)
```

Points to raise if nobody does:

- **Oceania has two countries.** A box plot of two points is not a
  distribution; "the lowest in Oceania" is New Zealand at 80.2 years.
- **Asia, not Africa, has the widest range** (Afghanistan 43.8 to Japan
  82.6). A title written from the AI's prior — "most unequal in Africa" — is
  wrong; a title written from `count()` and `summarise()` is not.
- **Turkey is the lowest in Europe** — a classification in the data, not a
  fact about the world. Check how the data define a continent.
- **Swaziland** is the 2007 name (Eswatini since 2018) — the AI may "correct"
  it and then the label no longer matches the data.

# Sharing (15 min)

Put a two-column table on the board: route P / route T, minutes to a chart
the pair would hand in. Then the four questions on the slide. Steer towards:

1. **Time:** route T is usually as fast or faster — for people who know the
   template. That is the trade-off: good AI use needs the same knowledge.
2. **Worse outcomes:** collect concrete examples from round 1 (wrong data,
   invented file, made-up claim).
3. **Own knowledge:** which geom shows variation, what `n` is, which numbers
   to trust.
4. **Next time:** templates for routine charts; AI for small syntax
   questions and for explaining errors.
